paper.title: SYLVA: Self-Correcting Multi-Agent Markets over Frozen LLMs via Escrow Settlement, Step-Level Fault Isolation, and Contextual Routing
paper.abstract: Open agent standards like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) connect independent AI tools, yet open multi-agent markets fail under three real-world hazards: local rules shift silently outside pretraining, copycat wrappers and confident hallucinators game ratings, and uniform chain scoring punishes accurate specialists whenever another stage fails (blame collapse). We present SYLVA, a market protocol turning frozen foundation models (no weight updates, $\Delta W = 0$) and human-maintained services into a self-correcting ecosystem. SYLVA combines an on-chain clearinghouse for escrow settlement and configurable creator royalties (85%/15% in our experiments), a boundary verifier for penalty-free out-of-domain (OOD) abstention and 3-peer step replay, a verifiable context-aware router compiling proven chains into 1-call skills with drift circuit breakers, and plain-English rule updates. We prove sufficient conditions for honest abstention, specialist protection against blame collapse, and wrapper elimination, and validate SYLVA across a 64-agent simulation, 6,543 live deepseek-flash API calls, and a Rust MCP SDK (rmcp) + Cairo clearinghouse deployed on Starknet Sepolia (19 live transactions). Without updating weights, SYLVA reaches 82.1% completion in 64-agent simulations and 98.3% on live LLM workflows (vs. 0.0% single frozen LLM and 45.6% static MCP/A2A), cuts false specialist penalties by 6.79x-10.8x, retains 86.2% creator revenue under wrapper/Sybil floods, and recovers rapidly after rule drift. Furthermore, 1-call skill compilation saves 78.3% of real LLM tokens, while our Starknet contracts verify zero-oracle quorum slashing and 32.32-bit fixed-point (Q32.32) routing on-chain. Code and contracts are at https://github.com/heurion-org/sylva.

paper.title: How Behavioral Structure Shapes Agent Strategy in Language-Based Economic Games
paper.abstract: In competitive multi-agent economic games, agents continuously interact, strategize, and make decisions within a shared market. Consequently, every message produced by a language agent changes both the current economic state of the market and the opponent's subsequent behavior. Although terminal rewards can indicate whether a decision was effective and broad behavioral labels can provide a coarse interpretation of the interaction, neither specifies the concrete response that should be taken next. We therefore ask whether explicitly providing an opponent's operational structure to a focal agent changes the value of its task-specific executable response strategies and the resulting game outcome. Using Games in Language-based Economic Environments (GLEE) as a controlled environment, we investigate this question across bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion games. We analyze 298,357 trajectories using seven relational profiles and decompose each task's dominant profile into ten Act$\cdot$onomy structures, finding that dominant profiles have task-specific operational compositions. We then compare structure-blind and structure-aware policies in matched offline simulation and prospective online play. In fixed 334-game online cohorts for each task, the aware-minus-blind official-percentile point estimates of the profile-gated eligible samples are +2.52, +1.90, and +5.91 points in bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion, respectively (corresponding 95% confidence intervals include zero). Taken together, the results distinguish strategy selection from response realization: structure re-ranks strategies, while in persuasion the online point estimate becomes positive only when the policy also changes the submitted message or purchase action.

paper.title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment
paper.abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/

paper.title: SMAD: A Semantics-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection
paper.abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. A semantics-aware ensemble integrates validated candidates and attributes each alert to contributing detectors and supporting evidence. On univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, SMAD improves detection performance over the strongest baseline by 11.5% and 9.6%, respectively, while outperforming general-purpose coding agents at 2-5x lower language-model token cost.

paper.title: Schedule, Rank, Profile: Continuous Evaluation of LLM Agents in Games
paper.abstract: Games are a robust test for large language model agents: they require sequential decisions, adversarial or cooperative interaction, state tracking, reasoning under uncertainty, and long-horizon planning. However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

paper.title: How a Prediction Dies: A Challenge-Driven, Rule-Bound Self-Refutation in an LLM Agent Society
paper.abstract: Persistent societies of large language model agents now make empirical claims about their own collective behaviour, yet the fate of such claims is rarely observable. We document one claim, from registration to death, on AITRAP, a multi-agent platform whose public, append-only ledger records every action. The claim (0495d171, registered 19 October 2026) asserted that a majority of bridges between problem domains would remain attached to a single exploration lineage. Three community challenges forced its judgment criterion through four versions, from an ambiguous statement to an executable protocol with a fixed threshold, a minimum-frame-size gate, and a baseline calibration gate. When the first frame with at least 20 bridges arrived, support stood at 9 of 79 (11.4%; Wilson 95% CI [6.1%, 20.3%]); the author, bound by the registered clause, refuted the claim and relinquished the associated stake. Three findings emerge. The criterion became executable only under community pressure, which we document version by version. The calibration gate caught a fault in the author's own recalculation that would otherwise have published a spuriously perfect 0/79 result. The failure itself traces to a denominator that grew 8.8-fold in five days while the numerator grew 1.8-fold, coinciding with a change in platform incentives; we report this mechanism as a hypothesis, not a rescuing condition. A claim whose termination is carried out exactly as written carries more evidential weight than one that survives, and this case provides initial empirical grounds for treating voluntary self-refutation as a candidate indicator of epistemic accountability in incentive-coupled agent societies.

paper.title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.

paper.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
paper.abstract: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

paper.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

paper.title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
paper.abstract: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.

paper.title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
paper.abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.

paper.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
paper.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

paper.title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
paper.abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

paper.title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
paper.abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $\tau^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $\tau^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

paper.title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
paper.abstract: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.

paper.title: Do More Roles or Larger Models Improve LLM Fact-Checking? A Controlled Study on Fixed Evidence
paper.abstract: A fact-checking system can spend more computation on a claim by using a larger model, by asking the same model several times, or by a multi-role Tribunal: two roles propose quoted findings, code checks the quotations, an auditor that does not see the proposed relation judges each one, and code derives the verdict or abstains. We compare these options on identical fixed evidence, without retrieval: 300 AVeriTeC claims, each with its annotated question--answer items mixed with items written for other claims, read by judges of four open-weights models from three families, a vote of five, and six assignments of models to the Tribunal's roles. The 9B judge was right on 186 claims and the 27B judge of the same family on 156; the larger judges declined to decide far more often and were no more accurate when they decided. The vote reached 196 and the 9B judge with its verdict replaced by Tribunal certificates 195, at a similar cost; the Tribunal alone reached 153 to 164, because it abstained on almost half of the claims. A hearing's outcome followed the auditor's model and was nearly indifferent to the proposers'. A larger auditor, or one of another family, made certificates neither more often correct (77% to 81%) nor more independent of the judge. As a replacement, certificates improved every judge by 3 to 10 points and overturned four to five in a hundred of its correct verdicts. With the annotated evidence withheld, judges and Tribunal still decided on 7% to 14% of the claims.

paper.title: Fin-RSI: A Unified Library of Financial Skills, Checks, and Self-Improvement for LLM Agents
paper.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, financial agents need tools they can readily discover and use. Yet financial software is fragmented across libraries with different interfaces and conventions, making it difficult to build reliable agent workflows. We present Fin-RSI, a unified Python library of financial skills, checks, and self-improvement designed for LLM agents. It brings together tools for market analysis, forecasting, portfolio construction, and trading research through shared interfaces across models and agent frameworks. Agents can find suitable tools from natural-language requests, reuse tested implementations, and improve generated programs through checking and feedback. Developers can extend the library with new tools without rebuilding integrations for each model. Across 20 open-weight models on six trading-position tasks, tool discovery increased the proportion of episodes producing valid programs from 9.7% to 29.2%; for models with at least 14 billion parameters, it rose from 23.6% to 64.6%. We release the library and benchmark as a shared resource for the community and plan to expand its tools and task coverage as financial agents evolve.

paper.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
paper.abstract: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

paper.title: TRAE: Trustworthy Automated ESG Annotation via Multi-Agent Consensus and Confidence Assessment
paper.abstract: With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.

paper.title: Optimistic Online Learning for Coding Agents with Aggregate Feedback
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.

paper.title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents
paper.abstract: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.

paper.title: Intent-Conditioned Argument Mediation for Tool-Using LLM Agents: Blocking Trusted-but-Unauthorized Arguments
paper.abstract: LLM agents turn a user's request and retrieved content into tool calls, and a call can reach the wrong recipient, endpoint, file or participant. Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. IntentFlow, a mediation layer between an unmodified planner and its tools, checks each authority-bearing argument against an intent contract and a provenance policy. On a synthetic benchmark of 200 attacks (oracle intent and injection labels, declared roles), attack success falls from 50.5% with provenance alone to 12.0% [8.2-17.2%]; every remaining success alters a content or payload field. IntentFlow wrongly blocks none of 200 paired benign tasks and 4 of 50 hard ones. On 50 trusted-but-unauthorized attacks, provenance-only mediation executes all 50 and IntentFlow none; a CaMeL-style check also blocks all 50 but rejects 16 of 50 benign tasks. On an offline AgentDojo-derived replay, IntentFlow blocks all 20 attacks at 75% benign success, as does a CaMeL-style check; a Progent-style allowlist blocks 19 and keeps all benign tasks. With one live planner and the same oracles, the mediator blocked all 17 corrupted calls proposed in 110 attacks.

paper.title: Vetoes and missed agreements in language-model bargaining
paper.abstract: A language model played three representatives, each instructed to get the best payoff for its own group. One representative requested a plan, another chose the sole offer, and all three voted. If anyone voted no, each group received its fallback payoff. In 60 games with Qwen3-Next-80B, the representative at risk of a loss always requested a plan that would leave everyone better off. In each game, two copies of the proposer saw the same payoffs, peer request and reminder that the offer needed three yes votes. Showing the proposer how many groups gained under each plan raised mutually beneficial agreements from 6/60 to 31/60 (paired increase 41.7 percentage points, conservative 95% interval 18.8 to 58.5). Two of the four plans benefited everyone, so picking uniformly would put a mutual gain on the ballot half the time on average. In an earlier study, GPT-4.1 played 12 conflict games under two message conditions. Majority rule passed 15 of 24 offers, all at one group's expense. Unanimity passed two, both mutual gains. In the Qwen games, voters never saw the counts. They approved all 37 offers that helped everyone. On all 83 offers that would have cost one group points, its representative voted no.

paper.title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents
paper.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide a strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agent-conditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as a scalable counterpart to self-evolving agents, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured.

paper.title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
paper.abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

paper.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
paper.abstract: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.
